===== FILE 20479__1.pdf =====
September 3, 2025 
 
Director, Office of Regulation Policy and Management (00REG) 
Department of Veterans Affairs,  
810 Vermont Avenue, NW, Room 1064 
Washington, DC 20420 
 
RE:   Proposed Rule on Reproductive Health Services 
 (RIN 2900-AS31) 
FR Document 2025-14687 
Citation: 90 FR 36415 
 
DAV (Disabled American Veterans) is pleased to respond to the Department of Veterans 
Affairs (VA) notice of the Proposed Rule on Reproductive Health Services, as published in the 
Federal Register on August 4, 2025. 
 
SUMMARY AND BACKGROUND: 
 
The VA is proposing to significantly limit access to abortion services and abortion 
counseling in its medical benefits package by reverting applicable regulations (38 CFR 17.38 and 
17.272) to their pre-2022 iteration, which only included an exception for abortions to be 
provided by VA or paid for through the Civilian Health and Medical Program of the Department 
of Veterans Affairs (CHAMPVA) if the life of the pregnant woman was endangered. DAV 
opposes this rule. 
 
In September 2022, following the Supreme Court’s issuance of the Dobbs v. Jackson 
Women's Health Organization, VA issued an Interim Final Rule (IFR) (87 FR 55287, September 
9, 2022) that expanded the instances in which abortions could be performed or paid for to 
include abortions for women when the pregnancy was the result of rape or incest, or because the 
pregnant woman’s health would be endangered if the pregnancy were carried to term. The 2022 
IFR also removed the exclusion of abortion counseling for VA health care providers as well as 
CHAMPVA providers.  
 
The newly proposed rule would reinstate the prior exclusion on abortion coverage, only 
allowing an exception when the life of the pregnant woman would be endangered. It would also 
exclude all abortion counseling services by VA and through CHAMPVA. 
 
COMMENTS 
 
DAV is a congressionally chartered and VA-accredited veterans service organization 
(VSO) with nearly a million veteran members, all of whom have been disabled, injured or made 
ill during wartime service. We are dedicated to ensuring that veterans, their families, caregivers, 

2 
 
and survivors can access the full range of benefits and services available to them, to include 
high-quality, comprehensive health care and specialized and gender-specific programs for both 
men and women. For women veterans specifically, we advocate to ensure access to 
comprehensive services to meet their unique health care needs, including reproductive care 
services, inclusive of counseling and psychological services related to combat exposure, intimate 
partner violence or sexual trauma.  
 
Since the creation of VA’s modern medical benefits package in 1999, as required by the 
Veterans’ Health Care Eligibility Reform Act of 1996 (Public Law 104-262), until the issuance 
of the IFR in September 2022, VA has generally had a prohibition against providing or paying 
for abortion services and abortion counseling, allowing an exception only when the life of the 
pregnant woman would be endangered. However, VA’s long held policy on abortion has not 
been consistent with other federal health care programs that are generally bound by the Hyde 
Amendment, an amendment to federal appropriations bills that prohibits the use of federal funds 
for abortions. Since 1993, the Hyde Amendment has included exceptions for instances of rape 
and incest, or when the life of the pregnant woman is in danger. These exceptions have applied 
to most federal health care and insurance programs, including the Department of Defense 
(DOD), Federal Bureau of Prisons, federal employee health benefits, Medicaid, Indian Health 
Service and others.  
 
However, the proposed rule would not include the exceptions for rape or incest, 
consistent with the longstanding Hyde Amendment. In practice, this could mean a female service 
member who was raped prior to transitioning out of military service, and who learns she is 
pregnant after enrolling in the VA health care system, would not be covered by VA to have an 
abortion. Had she still been on active duty, DOD would have paid or performed the abortion; if 
she worked for VA, her federal employee health insurance would have paid for the abortion; and 
even if she was serving time in a federal prison, her abortion would have been covered. 
However, as an enrollee in the VA health care system, she would not have been covered even for 
an abortion resulting from rape.  
 
We also note that earlier this year on January 25, the President issued an executive order 
called “Enforcing the Hyde Amendment” which it described it as “…established, commonsense 
policy…”  and called for federal policy to be “…consistent with the Hyde Amendment…” 
However, as discussed above, the proposed rule is not consistent with the Hyde Amendment.  
 
We recognize that abortion is a deeply sensitive issue that elicits strong views by 
Americans from different backgrounds and across the political spectrum. While public debate 
will continue, DAV’s responsibility is to ensure that policy decisions remain centered on the 
health, safety, and well-being of our nation’s wartime service-disabled veterans. 
 
Consistent with our constitution, bylaws and adopted resolutions, we believe that medical 
services available to veterans through the VA medical benefits package should not be reduced or 
taken away as a result of regulatory or legislative changes. Any policy changes proposed must 
put veterans’ health and safety first—especially for women veterans who may face complex 
reproductive health challenges requiring timely, expert care. VA must continue expanding 

3 
 
gender-specific and comprehensive services to meet the needs of the growing women veteran 
population. For all of the aforementioned reasons, DAV opposes the proposed rule. 
 
Whenever VA pursues changes to its medical benefits package, it must work closely with 
veterans and veteran stakeholders in developing such changes, and must provide clear and 
consistent guidance to veterans, providers, and Congress to ensure new or modified policies are 
applied safely across the system. Stakeholders should work together, as we have on many past 
issues, to preserve VA’s capacity to deliver high-quality, comprehensive care. 
 
DAV will continue to advocate for equitable, timely access to safe, high-quality care for 
all veterans. We remain committed to working together with Congress, VA, and our VSO 
partners to strengthen and sustain the VA health care system so that VA remains the primary 
provider and coordinator of health care for enrolled veterans. 
 
Sincerely,  
 
 
 
Joy J. Ilem 
National Legislative Director
